transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Dr. Arjun Sethi (CTO, Elysium), Priya Rao (ML Lead), Carlos Mendes (Infra), Sophie Lee (Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick round robin - from our side it's maya and liam. from elysium?
[00:06] Dr. Arjun Sethi: arjun here, hi.
[00:07] Priya Rao: priya.
[00:08] Carlos Mendes: carlos.
[00:09] Sophie Lee: sophie.
[00:12] Maya Chen: great. agenda is a quantization deep dive focused on runtime perf, latency/throughput, kv cache behavior, and accuracy regressions we've seen with 8-bit and awq style quant methods. liam will drive the tech section.

[00:30] Liam Patel: cool thanks. quick context — elysium mentioned you're running a 13B/70B mix for assistive control and logs, and you need sub-200ms p95 for short chat-style prompts in our hosted evaluation, and also want to move to on-prem for sensitive telemetry. is that right?
[00:42] Priya Rao: yeah that's right. our 13B is the workhorse, 70B is for planning and occasionally heavy reasoning. latency for 13B is more critical. our perf target is 150-200 ms p95 for 13B in normal mode.
[00:55] Liam Patel: ok. so we'll discuss three families: FP16/FP8 simulated, INT8 (post-training quant), and GPTQ/AWQ family which are more aggressive per-layer quant strategies. quick note: 'AWQ' in literature sometimes conflates weight-only quant with per-channel scaling; our internal AWQ variant here is the one optimized for latency on ampere-like GPUs and some CPU inference stacks.

[01:20] Dr. Arjun Sethi: can we start with accuracy tradeoffs — what signatures should we expect if we go from fp16 to int8/gptq/awq? priya sort of saw some hallucination uptick in earlier tests.
[01:31] Liam Patel: yeah, good question. intuitive summary: INT8 (naive symmetric or asymmetric) tends to preserve most generation quality for backbone tasks if you calibrate with representative data, but tends to show degradation on rare token prediction and tail cases — you might see higher perplexity on out-of-distribution prompts. GPTQ, because it does per-layer quantization with second-order correction, usually gives better accuracy than naive INT8 for the same bitwidth, but it's slower to produce and may require per-model calibration artifacts. AWQ often matches GPTQ quality or slightly better on some models, and has a kernel-friendly layout that can be faster on CPU, but can still show small deltas in probability of low-frequency tokens.

[02:10] Priya Rao: that matches our feeling — the logs we ran showed correct majority answers but a few edge-case planning prompts returned odd steps. could be tokenization differences also.

[02:20] Liam Patel: yep tokenization mismatch is common; also KV cache layout changes sometimes alter beam-search timing which can expose race conditions in prompt concatenation. we'll check that.

[02:30] Sophie Lee: we saw a 2-3% accuracy drop on our regression suite when using GPTQ 4-bit heuristics, but it was concentrated in specific eval sets (nav planning). how worrying is that?
[02:41] Liam Patel: depends on your success criteria. 2-3% on an aggregate metric might hide a 10-15% drop on critical slices. recommended approach: run per-slice eval and threshold-based gating. if those slices are business-critical, either keep FP16 for rollout or use mixed precision (e.g., keep some attention/projection layers at higher precision).

[03:05] Dr. Arjun Sethi: mixed precision — is that something Redwood runtime supports today? and would that complicate deployment on-prem?
[03:12] Maya Chen: short answer: yes, Redwood runtime supports mixed precision layer pinning and variant routing. on-prem we can include the same runtime and kernel set — but you'll need the optimized ops compiled for your target CPU/GPU. liam?

[03:24] Liam Patel: yeah, runtime supports per-layer dtype selection and we ship build artifacts for common CPU instruction sets and NVIDIA/AMD GPUs. for on-prem we can either provide a container with precompiled kernels (if your hardware matches our build matrix) or we can cross-compile against your exact setup. that influences the onboarding time.

[03:45] Carlos Mendes: our infra is Ampere A10G on-prem for inference. we also have a couple of AMD MI250s in research. kernel compatibility is a real concern.

[03:52] Liam Patel: A10G is covered; AWQ/GPTQ kernels have good perf there. MI250 might need extra tuning — we can bring in the compile infra but it'll be a small project.

[04:05] Maya Chen: let's pivot to KV cache and batching — you mentioned interactive prompts with prefix caching?

[04:12] Priya Rao: we do prefix caching for device telemetry prompts, prefix length ~512 tokens typically, but many of our calls are short follow-ups where KV cache reuse could help. the problem we saw was sometimes latency spikes when cache hits were expected.

[04:27] Liam Patel: common causes: cache invalidation due to model variant mismatch (e.g., if a canary uses different quantization layout), and memory pressure kicking out cached segments. also quantized kernels sometimes change KV layout — especially weight-only quant methods can reorder parameters which necessitates runtime-level compatibility layers.

[04:45] Priya Rao: so if we deploy GPTQ and AWQ variants, will cache be compatible? we want seamless fallback between hosted and on-prem and between quant variants for graceful degradation.

[04:56] Liam Patel: we recommend a canonical cache key that includes model id + quantization scheme + kernel fingerprint. Redwood runtime's smart routing uses that to ensure cache reuse only when layout-compatible. for graceful fallback you can allow prefix re-encoding (costly) or maintain a small warm pool of canonical fp16 instances for cache priming.

[05:20] Sophie Lee: ok that makes sense. what about batching policies? we're sensitive to P95 latency.

[05:27] Liam Patel: batching is a tradeoff: larger batches increase throughput and lower per-token cost but increase tail latency. we have dynamic batching with per-route latency SLOs — essentially we will hold a request up to X ms to accumulate a batch. for your 150-200ms p95 target on 13B we can tune hold time to maybe 10-20 ms and use smaller max-batch sizes. also kernel-level continuous batching (packing micro-batches into fused matmul) helps. but quantized kernels sometimes change the optimal micro-batch size.

[06:00] Dr. Arjun Sethi: can Redwood runtime do on-device continuous KV caching with batching? like keep the KV cache warm across short lived sessions?

[06:08] Liam Patel: yes, we support long-lived session handles with pinned KV cache. memory limits apply — we provide autoshrink policies and LRU eviction. note: on multi-tenant Dedicated pools we isolate caches per-customer; on bare-metal on-prem it's whatever you provision.

[06:30] Maya Chen: let's talk numbers — Liam, do you have comparison stats for latency and throughput for FP16 vs GPTQ vs AWQ on a 13B model?

[06:36] Liam Patel: i do — rough ballpark from our test harness on A10G: FP16 ~ 60 tokens/s, p50 latency for a 32-token generation ~ 40 ms; GPTQ int4 variant improves tokens/s to ~110 tokens/s but p95 latency has a heavier tail, p95 ~ 210 ms for same 32-token workload if you don't tune batching; AWQ tuned kernel is ~100-120 tokens/s with p95 ~160-180ms. INT8 weight-only (naive) sits between FP16 and GPTQ in throughput but with variable accuracy. these numbers change with prompt length and KV reuse.

[07:20] Priya Rao: that aligns with our bench — we saw AWQ slightly better p95 than GPTQ in our initial runs. were those runs using same sequence lengths?
[07:26] Liam Patel: yes same seq length, but we saw variability when KV cache reuse was high — GPTQ's memory layout led to slightly larger kernel launch variance causing tail spikes.

[07:40] Carlos Mendes: what's the debug approach for tail latency spikes? we saw occasional 400ms p95 despite average being low.

[07:47] Liam Patel: typical steps: enable per-request tracing (we have a trace hook), capture kernel launch times, check for memory thrashing/evictions, and confirm that workload didn't trigger a fallback to FP16 for some shards. we'll also check RPC scheduling queues. Redwood Console can show token-level breakdowns; we can correlate with your system metrics.

[08:10] Sophie Lee: about accuracy regressions we've seen — are there automated eval gates Redwood recommends before promoting a quant variant? like thresholds by slice?

[08:18] Liam Patel: yes, we recommend three gates: global metric delta (e.g., <1% drop aggregated), critical-slice delta (e.g., <2% on user-defined slices), and behavior test pass rate (binary tests for safety/constraint prompts). we can run Redwood Optimize to propose quantization profiles and then auto-generate eval reports per-slice.

[08:40] Dr. Arjun Sethi: what's the size of the calibration dataset for GPTQ? do we need thousands of tokens? and can we generate from our telemetry while preserving privacy?

[08:49] Liam Patel: GPTQ benefits from representative calibration but it's surprisingly robust with a few thousand sequences if they're representative. for privacy you can run calibration entirely on-prem; we provide a calibration tool that runs locally and outputs small numeric artifacts (no raw telemetry leaves your network).

[09:05] Priya Rao: good. one other question — spike in hallucinations seemed correlated with certain attention patterns; are there known layers that are more sensitive and should be kept at fp16?

[09:15] Liam Patel: attention output projections and some early embedding layers are often sensitive; likewise final language model head and layernorms can be higher-impact. mixed precision pinning those layers can recover most of the delta with small perf cost. we can present a suggested layer list after we run a graded sensitivity analysis.

[09:36] Maya Chen: quick note — we'll share a spreadsheet with the per-layer sensitivity heuristics and suggested pinning for your model.

[09:42] Sophie Lee: one more infra question: KMS/HSM integration for on-prem — we need to keep key material in our HSM, but also let Redwood runtime decrypt model weights at load. what's the pattern?

[09:53] Maya Chen: common pattern: customer-managed KMS/HSM decrypts model artifact into memory space on the node, Redwood runtime reads decrypted weights from memfs. we support integration with HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS (on dedicated), and direct HSM APIs. we don't persist keys; we only accept a short-lived unwrap token. Carlos, does that fit your security posture?

[10:10] Carlos Mendes: yes that's acceptable. we'll need the exact API contract.

[10:15] Liam Patel: also, for air-gapped installs we can provide an offline signing step and a local decryptor.

[10:22] Dr. Arjun Sethi: ok great. back to tests — timeline: can you run a 13B AWQ/GPTQ comparison on our sample workload next week? and include per-slice accuracy and per-token cost estimates?

[10:31] Maya Chen: yes — action items listed. liam will run the on-prem tests once carlos provisions the node. we'll also share the benchmark spreadsheet and the runtime build options.

[10:40] Priya Rao: expected regression thresholds — for critical nav planning slices we need <1% drop, otherwise we keep fp16. is that doable?

[10:48] Liam Patel: we can aim for that. if mixed precision still doesn't hit the threshold, we recommend model distillation or keeping a small fp16 path for those slices.

[10:58] Sophie Lee: last thing — what about model rollout strategy? gradual canary between quant variants?

[11:04] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B and automatic fallback. Canary can be traffic-based (percent) or slice-based (route specific prompts). we can configure an automated rollback if slice error increases beyond thresholds.

[11:18] Dr. Arjun Sethi: perfect. thanks everyone. any outstanding risks?

[11:22] Liam Patel: main risks: on-prem kernel compatibility delays, and edge-case accuracy regressions on safety-critical slices. both manageable with our recommended gating and mixed precision strategies.

[11:32] Maya Chen: recap / next steps: 1) liam run GPTQ vs AWQ perf runs on Elysium workload and upload to shared drive by 11/12; 2) maya share security/KMS and VPC deployment docs by 11/07; 3) carlos provision node by 11/10 and give se access. we'll set up a follow-up sync after results.

[11:50] Dr. Arjun Sethi: sounds good. thanks.

[11:52] Maya Chen: thanks all, talk soon.

Notes (auto): transcription contains some mis-heard tokens, speaker attribution may have small errors. shared artifacts: "GPTQ_vs_AWQ_elysium_benchmarks.xlsx" (internal drive link), "redwood-onprem-kms-checklist.pdf" (link).
